passage: The review meeting at the ward office ended, and Hemant sat back down with the composting report open. 'Total flop,' he muttered. Omkar, from the accounts desk, pulled up a chair. 'Flop out of ten, or flop out of what?' Hemant almost laughed. On the whiteboard he drew a line from 0 to 10. Collection from the two big colonies: steady every week, so maybe a 7. Bins in the market lane: broken twice, smelly, a 3. Volunteer turnout: strong for a month, then gone, a 4. He wrote two columns, Kept Going and Fell Apart, and the second was shorter than he expected. 'So it's a five, not a zero,' Omkar said. Hemant circled the market lane. 'And this is what the next round fixes first.'

qa.q: Which part of the composting drive did Hemant give a 3?
qa.a: The bins in the market lane, which broke twice and were smelly, got a 3.

qa.q: Why did 'total flop' feel true to Hemant right after the review meeting?
qa.a: Hemant was frustrated and discouraged after the meeting, so the problems filled his mind and one bad part seemed to stand for the whole drive.

qa.q: What choice turned Hemant's review from a verdict into a plan?
qa.a: Drawing a 0-to-10 line and making two columns let him score each part on its own, so he could see the colonies were working and pick the market lane as the first fix.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Hemant's shift from 'flop' to 'five'?
qa.a: Omkar likely finds this far more useful: a flat 'flop' gave the team nothing to act on, while a five with one clear first fix gives everyone a next step.

grounding: Shows an adult who dismissed a whole project as a flop rescoring each part on a 0-to-10 line and finding a middle rating with a clear next step.

passage:
Dear Shalini,
On Sunday night I typed 'the book fair was a disaster' to you and then deleted it. I'm glad I did. This morning I tried your trick and gave it a mark out of ten instead.
Footfall: 6. We hoped for four hundred people and about two hundred and fifty came.
Stalls: 8. Every publisher we invited showed up.
Food counter: 2. It ran out by noon and the queue got angry.
Clash with the football final: 1, and that one's on me for not checking.
Then I made two lists, keep and change. The keep list is longer, which surprised me. The children's reading corner was full all day. So maybe a 6 overall, not a zero. Next year I check the sports calendar first.
Love,
Lalremsiami

qa.q: How many people came to the book fair?
qa.a: About two hundred and fifty people came, against the four hundred that were hoped for.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling on Sunday night when typing that the fair was a disaster?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was probably tired and let down 😔, and the angry food queue loomed so large that the whole day felt ruined. Deleting the message hints that part of Lalremsiami already doubted that verdict.

qa.q: Which choice helped Lalremsiami judge the fair more fairly, and why?
qa.a: Scoring each part out of ten and making keep and change lists split one big feeling into pieces, which showed the stalls and reading corner had gone well and pointed to one clear fix: check the sports calendar.

qa.q: If you were Shalini reading this email, what might you notice?
qa.a: Shalini would see that the trick was actually used and that Lalremsiami came away with a plan instead of a label, which might make Shalini glad to have shared it.

grounding: Shows an adult replacing the word 'disaster' with part-by-part marks out of ten and keep and change lists, landing on a middle score that leaves room to improve.

passage: People kept asking me, 'Bhupen, how did the screening go?' And I kept saying, 'Total waste of a year.' Alka, I said it at the bus stop, I said it to Ma, I said it to the mirror. Then my editor asked me one question: 'Waste out of ten?' I couldn't answer. So that night I sat down and went scene by scene. Sound: a 3, honestly, the wind ruins the market scenes. The old boatman's interview: a 9, the hall went silent during it. Colour, pacing, the ending: all somewhere in the middle, fives and sixes. I made two lists on the back of the ticket stub, what stays in my next film and what never happens again. And the funny thing? Once it wasn't a zero, I stopped hiding the film. I sent it to two more festivals last week.

qa.q: Which part of the film did Bhupen give a 9?
qa.a: The old boatman's interview got a 9, because the hall went silent during it.

qa.q: Why did 'total waste of a year' feel like the honest answer to Bhupen at first?
qa.a: Right after the screening the bad sound was the loudest memory, and one harsh verdict felt safer than hoping and being disappointed again. Saying it first also meant nobody else could say it.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Bhupen, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: The editor's question 'Waste out of ten?' pushed Bhupen to score scene by scene, and once the film was no longer a zero, Bhupen stopped hiding it and sent it to two more festivals.

qa.q: How might the editor feel on hearing the film went out to two more festivals?
qa.a: The editor would probably feel relieved and glad 😊 that one small question pulled a year of shared work out of the drawer.

grounding: Shows a young adult who called a film a total waste rating each part on a ten-point scale and listing what to keep and what to change, which reopens the project.

passage:
My roommate Nilesh spent two months planning his first home-bakery stall at the Sunday flea market in Pune. On the day, it drizzled, half the crowd never came, and he carried three boxes of unsold brownies back up our stairs.

"Total disaster," he said, dropping onto the sofa. "I'm not a baker. I'm a guy who wasted two months."

Then he went quiet and frowned at the ceiling. "No. Disaster is too big a word." He took a flattened pizza box and drew a line from one to ten. Sales: four. The lemon cake sold out in an hour, so that was a nine. Stall set-up: two, because the banner kept blowing into people's faces. Price cards: seven.

I didn't say much. I just watched him make two lists, "Keep" and "Change", in black marker. The "Keep" list was longer.

"So maybe a five," he said. "And next time, a heavier banner and more lemon cake."

— Tarun

qa.q: What sold out in an hour at Nilesh's stall?
qa.a: The lemon cake sold out in an hour.

qa.q: Why did "total disaster" feel accurate to Nilesh as he dropped onto the sofa?
qa.a: He was tired, wet and carrying three boxes of unsold brownies, so the losses were all he could see. After two months of planning, anything less than success felt like wasted time.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did the scale help?
qa.a: The turning point was when Nilesh caught himself and said disaster was too big a word. Rating each part from one to ten showed what worked, like the lemon cake, and gave clear fixes for next time.

qa.q: How might Tarun have felt watching Nilesh go from "disaster" to "maybe a five"?
qa.a: Tarun was probably relieved to see a friend stop beating himself up without needing to be argued out of it. Staying quiet and just watching let Nilesh do the rethinking himself.

grounding: A roommate watches a young man catch himself calling his market stall a disaster, then rate each part on a scale and list what worked and what to change.

passage:
Friday: Charu pressed "submit" at 11:52 p.m. Her bus-shelter design for the city competition had taken four months of evenings. She lay awake picturing her name on the winners' board.

Monday, 10 a.m.: The list came out. Not even shortlisted. Charu closed her laptop. "It was all rubbish. Four months of rubbish," she told Lavanya at the next desk, and went to stand at the office window for a long time.

Wednesday evening: At home, Charu opened the file again, mostly to delete it. Instead she caught her own words: all rubbish. Was it? She made a grid. Idea: eight out of ten; the rainwater roof was good. Drawings: six. Cost estimate: three, rushed at the end. Written statement: four, too long.

She wrote at the bottom: "Next time, start the costing in month two." Then she saved the file under a new name: "Round 2".

qa.q: What did Charu give the rainwater roof idea?
qa.a: Charu gave the idea eight out of ten.

qa.q: What might Charu have been feeling as she stood at the office window for a long time?
qa.a: She was probably crushed and embarrassed after four months of evenings, and her words suggest she felt the whole effort was worthless. Standing alone gave her space to hide it.

qa.q: Which choice on Wednesday changed what Charu took from the competition?
qa.a: Instead of deleting the file, she questioned her own phrase "all rubbish" and graded each part. That showed a strong idea and a weak cost estimate, which she can fix next time.

qa.q: What would change if Lavanya had agreed on Monday that it was all rubbish?
qa.a: Charu might have deleted the file on Wednesday and never seen what was good about it. Lavanya's silence, at least, didn't lock in the harsh verdict.

grounding: Over three days a young woman goes from calling her competition entry all rubbish to grading its parts and noting what to change next time.
